description: The Open DS grammar: a finite set of questions a design system must answer. Reasons come first (business, people, content, tasks, human factors, outcomes, brand, use scenarios, team). Scopes follow, from typography to voice and tone. Every scope answers the same five method questions (roles, how many, how defined, values, lands in) and has the same parts: the tokens it owns, the components it lands in and its situations. Each scheme answers every question, and each answer says why and which earlier answers it follows from. Situations are the moments where people need to know what to use; each scheme answers them too. Component keys are the shared component API: every scheme fills every key its answers create.

scheme_order.why: The first three are shaped by what people do: scan and compare, read, finish the task. The last two are shaped by the brand: one loud brand, then many brands as themes, the most involved. Dense data comes first; it is the default everywhere.

ai.use_when: You need the list of questions behind a design system, or the meaning of a question id such as typography.definition or a situation id such as number-in-table.
ai.how_to_read: Reasons are answered first. A scope answer lists in 'because' the answers that pulled it. Scope question ids are <scope>.<method>, so typography.values and voice.values answer the same kind of question. Tokens follow from the answers. Components read only component keys. Written text in a scheme (voice, scenarios) lists in 'follows' the answers it was written from.

layers.description: Why the system exists: product, people, content, tasks, human factors, outcomes, brand, use scenarios, team.
The design decisions: typography, color, spacing, shape, elevation, motion, iconography, theming, accessibility, naming, voice and tone, components. Each answers the five method questions.
Primitives are the options; each option looks clearly different from the others (see options). Semantics are the decisions, in light and dark. Brands and modes are themes.
One key per component element, variant and state. Every scheme fills every key its answers create.

options.description: Rules every scheme's primitives follow. An option set exists to offer distinct choices, so each option looks clearly different from the others: two steps you cannot tell apart are one step. Prefer fewer steps that each do a job over one step per role. And keep only the options something reads: an option nothing reads is a choice nobody made.

used.say: outside color ramps, keep only the options a semantic, theme or component key reads
used.why: An option nothing reads is a choice nobody made. Color ramps stay whole, because a ramp is one unit with meaning.

rules.say: line heights are ratios of the text size, at least 0.2 apart
rules.why: A ratio follows each text's own size, and steps closer than 0.2 look the same.

methods.title: Roles
methods.description: Which roles the scope needs. Each role becomes a group of decisions.

methods.title: How many
methods.description: How many steps, levels or variants each role gets.

methods.title: How defined
methods.description: The rule that produces the values: a scale, a base unit, a style or a policy.

methods.title: Values
methods.description: Where the values sit, as a word. The exact values live in the tokens.

methods.title: Lands in
methods.description: Where the scope does its most visible work in the product.

reasons.title: Business and product
reasons.description: Why the product exists and what it does for the business. It frames every later answer.

questions.text: What does the product do for the business?
questions.description: The main job of the product. Operating tools, publishing, selling and public services pull the system in different directions.

questions.text: How many brands or products share the system?
questions.description: One brand keeps the system small. Many brands need a theming layer.

reasons.title: People and work context
reasons.description: Who uses the product, how often and with what abilities.

questions.description: The main audience. Experts learn an interface; occasional visitors must understand it at first sight.

questions.text: What accessibility level do we commit to?
questions.description: The accessibility promise. It sets floors for contrast, targets and states.

options.label: AA, with AAA where it is cheap

questions.description: Numbers, long text, forms and media each need different type, spacing and color.

questions.text: How much is on one screen?
questions.description: Information density. It drives spacing, type size and how groups separate.

reasons.title: Tasks and flows
reasons.description: What people do with the content.

questions.description: The task that must be fastest. Comparing, reading, completing and exploring need different layouts.

questions.text: How often do people repeat actions?
questions.description: Repetition. Frequent actions must be quiet and fast; rare ones can be explicit.
The scarce human resource on this product.

questions.text: How do people recall the interface?
questions.description: Learned interfaces can rely on recognition. Fresh visits need explicit labels.

options.label: They learn it and recognize it
They see it fresh each time

reasons.title: Outcomes
reasons.description: What success looks like and what failure costs.

questions.description: The measure the system optimises for.
The error the system must make hard.

reasons.title: Brand
reasons.description: How the brand should feel in the interface.

questions.text: What should the brand feel like?
How visible is the brand in the interface?
questions.description: How much brand expression the product carries.

questions.text: Which typefaces carry the product, and why?
questions.description: The faces for every text role, and how they meet what a typeface decision must consider: reading, range, brand and delivery.

options.label: A neutral grotesque, with a monospace for data
options.description: For products where numbers and records are the content.

options.label: A reading serif, with a sans for the interface
options.description: For long-form reading; the interface steps back.

options.label: One face drawn for legibility
options.description: For products where nobody may be left out.

options.description: For brands that lead with type.

considers.label: Readability
considers.ask: Does long text read easily at body size: open shapes, a comfortable x-height, even spacing?

considers.label: Legibility
considers.ask: Can people tell confusable characters apart, such as I, l and 1, or 0 and O, in data, codes and IDs?

considers.label: Scalability
considers.ask: Does it hold from the smallest caption to display, with a weight or an optical size for every role in the scale?

considers.label: Numerals
considers.ask: Do numbers read clearly and line up in tables?

considers.label: Scripts and languages
considers.ask: Does it cover every language the product ships, and what fills the gaps?

considers.label: Recognition
considers.ask: Do people know the product by its type?

considers.label: Familiarity
considers.ask: Does it feel known and trusted to its audience, not strange?

considers.label: Personality
considers.ask: Does it sound like the voice the brand answers ask for?

considers.label: Performance
considers.ask: How many families and files load, and is that in proportion?

considers.label: Licensing
considers.ask: Is it free to embed in apps and on the web, or what does it cost?

considers.label: Fallback and pairing
considers.ask: What shows before it loads or where it can't, and which face pairs with it?

reasons.title: Use scenarios
reasons.description: Where and for how long people use the product. Written scenarios follow from these answers.

questions.description: The place and device. A desk with a mouse, a phone on the move, or anything at all.
Session length. All-day use rewards learning; short visits must work at first sight.

reasons.title: Team and delivery
reasons.description: Who keeps the system right, and how fast it changes.

questions.description: Team size limits how many tokens and variants can stay correct.
Change rate. Fast change needs a stable component API and a flexible theme.

semantics.description: What each semantic key is for, written once for every scheme. Each entry says its intent, what to use it for, what not to use it for (and what to use instead) and, where it matters, which fills it may sit on and the contrast it must keep there. Words only; values come from each scheme. Every rule is checked.

key_colors.description: The page, its main surface and text, the main action at rest and on hover, and the focus ring: the colors that show a theme at a glance.

urgency.description: Status colors go up in urgency: info, then warning, then danger. Pick the level that matches the real risk. Never go up a level to get attention. Success sits outside the order.

keys.intent: The page background behind everything.

not_for.when: Cards and panels on the page

keys.intent: The base fill for content.
A fill one step above content, for parts that rise inside the page. In dark, one step lighter than content, so height reads by tone.

The fill of layers that float above the page: menus, popovers, dialogs, sheets and toasts. In dark, one step lighter than raised, so text, dividers and the ring on it keep their contrast. In light, white like raised: the shadow lifts it.

not_for.when: A part that rises inside the page

keys.intent: A recessed fill, a step below content.

not_for.when: An item the pointer or the keyboard is on

keys.intent: The fill of the item the pointer or the keyboard is on, or whose submenu is open. A state shows on the item's background, one step from the surfaces it sits on: darker in light, and darker in dark too, as raised layers take the lighter step.
The fill of an item while it is pressed. Where the scheme gives pressed its own value, one step past the highlight; where pressed reuses hover, the highlight's step.

tones.description: Text pairs with fills by tone. Every fill states its tone, light or dark, in each brand and mode: a decision, written on the fill as $extensions.open-ds.tone. Two text tokens serve every fill: color.text.on-light (the light mode's body text) on a light fill, color.text.on-dark (white) on a dark one, the same in both modes. Per-fill names (color.text.inverse, color.text.on-action, color.text.on-danger) point at the one their fill's tone picks. color.text.* and the page's own borders and focus ring are the mode's own set, for the page's own surfaces. Every fill is checked against what sits on it.

connections.description: How the tokens of a scope connect. comes-from: a token takes its value from another, a scale or a rule. pairs-with: two tokens keep a floor together, such as a fill and its text, or a box and the line it holds. stays-apart: two sets must not look alike, or must keep an order or a distance. Each one is checked in every brand and mode.

items.says: A soft fill comes from the hue of its own color: the same hue scale as its @.
A hover is the hue of its fill, one step on.
Surfaces, lines, page text, the secondary action and disabled read only steps of the neutral ramp.
The text on a fill is the text its fill's tone picks: on-light or on-dark.
Selection takes the hue of the main action, so a selected item reads as the brand's.
The scrim is the scheme's black, see-through, so it dims the page in both modes.

Every fill pairs with the text on it, by tone, and the pair keeps its contrast floor. A step number makes a promise: steps 400 apart give 3:1, 500 apart give 4.5:1, 700 apart give 7:1, in every hue of a scheme.

also.says: A tag's text on a category tint is the page's own text.

items.says: A category color has no meaning, so it never takes a status hue: a category in the warning hue reads as a warning.
the primary and danger fills stay at least 10 apart (ΔE in OKLab, ×100) in every brand and mode
items.why: A destructive commit must never look like the everyday one.

items.says: In dark mode the surfaces lighten as they rise: sunken, then default, then raised, then floating.
Each text size comes from one base and one ratio: base × ratio^step. Display, title and heading snap to the 4px grid; other text rounds to whole px.
Each line height comes from its role's line kind: the kind's ratio × the size, or a line box snapped to the kind's grid.
A control holds one label line: each control height is at least the label's line height, so the label never clips.
Each text size is at least one ratio step above the size on the step below it, so two roles never look almost alike.
The line kinds stay at least 0.2 apart (tight, snug, open), so each kind reads as its own.
items.why: Line heights closer than 0.2 look the same.

items.says: Each gap and inset comes from the spacing base: the base (4px for small steps, 8px for big ones) × the multiple of its use case.
Each step of the component spacing map comes from 4px × its multiplier × the scheme's rhythm, rounded to 4px and at most 64px. Held steps and the hairline stay fixed.
The gap between groups is at least twice the gap inside a group, so groups read as separate.
The gap between sections is at least 1.5 times the gap between groups, so a section reads as a larger break.
The gap between groups is at least the padding of a container, so content sits nearer its own edge than the next box.
A row is one default control tall, so a control in a row fills its height.
A row is at least the scheme's smallest target, so a clickable row is easy to hit.
A closing layer takes the feedback time, so an exit is as quick as the answer to a click.
An arriving layer eases out on the standard curve, so it comes to rest the way a state change does.
A panel takes at least the feedback time, so the eye can follow it from its trigger.
A launch moment takes at least the panel time, the step above panels.
Each control height comes from the control scale: the default, and compact and large a whole step below or above it.
An icon is at least one label line tall, so the icon and its label share one line.
The stroke, drawn on the icon set's 24px grid, renders at least 1px at the icon size, so thin lines do not break up.

neutral.description: The neutral scale. Primitives hold the grays below, each a whole ramp in light and dark. color.neutral.<step> is a semantic scale: each scheme or brand points it at one gray, recorded in its theme as neutral { gray, temperature, why, because }. Surfaces, borders, text, the secondary button and disabled read only color.neutral steps, never a gray directly. A scheme keeps only the gray it picked; this list is the menu.

grays.description: A cool blue-gray, barely tinted: reads as precise.
A deeper, bluer gray, about twice as tinted as slate: cool and firm.
No hue at all: nothing can lower contrast or carry a meaning.
A warm, yellowish gray, like paper.
A warm, rosy gray that sits under a vivid brand.

floor.description: One step below 0, for a scheme whose dark canvas sits on step 0: in dark, wells and the hover band take it, so they sit below the page. It is step 0 at 0.04 lower OKLab lightness, hue and chroma kept. In light it names step 0, as nothing sits above white, and no light role reads it.

variants.description: What the last part of a semantic name means, and the step it sits at on its hue scale. Every token ending in that part shares the meaning.

items.says: The color itself, at full strength: the mark, line or text that carries the role.
The soft, low-hierarchy version of a color: it sits quietly beside the other options and carries the palette's harmony into where it is used.
The same color one step on, so the pointer shows without a new meaning.

groups.description: What each group of a semantic name means. A token takes the meaning of every group in its name.

items.says: The colors a product uses, named by job, never by hue.
The gray ramp. Surfaces, lines and text take their steps from it.
The fills content sits on. Their lightness shows what is above what.
The colors of words and icons, each with the fill it sits on.
The colors of lines: dividers, control edges, the focus ring and selection.
The fills of things a person can do, by emphasis: primary, secondary and danger.
The main action of a view. One per view.
An action beside the main one, with less weight.
An action that destroys or cannot be undone.
Colors with a meaning: they tell a person the state of something.
Neutral news: something a person should know.
A task worked.
Something needs care before it goes wrong.
Something went wrong, or an action will destroy.
Colors with no meaning, for content that needs telling apart: decorative accents and non-semantic blocks such as tags, labels and chart series.
The shared look of controls that cannot be used right now.
The text roles. Each role sets its size, line height, weight and typeface.
The distances between and inside things.
The distance between items: it groups what is near and separates what is far.
The padding inside a box: it keeps content off the edge.
The fixed sizes of controls, rows, icons and hit areas.
The heights of controls: buttons, inputs and selects.
The corners: how round a shape is, by the job of the shape.
The thickness of lines.
How the keyboard's place shows.
The ring around the focused element: its width and its gap from the element.
The shadows that lift a layer above the page.
How things move: how long and on which curve.
How long a movement takes, by its job.
The curve of a movement: how it starts and how it stops.
How much shows through.
How icons are drawn.
The steps components space by: the base step times a multiplier, at this scheme's rhythm.

reason_form.description: Every reason in every scope takes this form, so a reader learns the job, how the property does it, what people get and which decision sets it.
reason_form.form: We use <value> for <role> in order to <job>. The <property> does this by <how it works>. So <what people get>, because <the decision in words> (<answer ids>).
reason_form.from_above: A value set from above names its mechanism in the job part: the scale it is a step of, the relation it follows, or the value it inherits.

parts.says: The job the value does, named from its property's jobs.
How the property itself does that job.
The decision in words; the reason's because list cites the answer ids.

trace.says: A text size exists because the roles answer names its role; the count answer sets how many steps the scale takes; the values answer sets the body size the scale grows from.
The definition answer sets how line heights follow the size: on the grid or in proportion.
Weight carries the hierarchy between roles (the scale answer), uses a weight the typeface draws well (the typeface answer), and stays legible at its size (the contrast floor).
Gaps and insets are the spacing roles; the definition answer sets the base step; the values answer sets the density, and so each use case's multiple of the base.

Decided: a row is one default control tall in every scheme. A row holds controls, so a taller row only adds a gap around them, and a shorter one cuts them. The target size answer sets the control height; the roles answer says whether rows are a decision of their own, and the values answer sets the density they follow.
The control corner is a decision: the corner answer, the brand's feel (tone) and the density answer.
The surface corner is a decision: the roles and count answers give containers their own corner, so touching cards read as separate objects, and the brand's feel sets its size (tone).
An option's corner is the surface corner minus the panel's padding (nesting), so it follows the surface's answers and the spacing answer.
A growing box takes the control corner, or the box corner when the control is a pill, so it follows the control corner's answers.
A badge takes the control corner unless the roles answer gives badges their own corner.
The layering answer says whether lines separate groups; the contrast floor says how heavy a line must be to be seen.
Focus is a state with its own look (roles answer); the ring is one step heavier than the default line, so it follows that line's answers too.
Focus is a state with its own look (roles answer); its gap is a fixed 2px in every scheme, for contrast: the page color between ring and control (W3C technique C40).
The roles answer names the layers that rise, each one step up the scale; the values answer sets the size of a step.
The values answer names how fast feedback feels.
A speed exists because the roles answer names its job; the count answer sets how many speeds there are.
The definition answer sets the easing: a standard ease-out or a spring.
The target-size answer sets the hit area: 24px for a pointer, 44px for touch. A control drawn smaller keeps its size; its hit area grows past it. The density answer says how close neighbours sit.
The values answer sets the target size, and the default control height follows it; compact and large are steps on the control scale below and above the default.
The values answer sets the icon size next to text; the count answer sets how many icon sizes exist.
The definition answer sets the icon style, and it names the stroke width.

A surface's step comes from the neutral ramp (the palette answer). The roles answer says what rises; the definition answer says if depth shows by tone or by lines; the modes answer sets the dark ladder.
A neutral step is a step of the neutral ramp (the palette answer); the modes answer sets the dark ramp.

A line's color is a neutral step (the palette answer). The definition answer says if lines separate groups; the modes answer sets the dark step; the contrast floor sets how strong a line that carries meaning is.

anatomy.description: The parts layer: the jobs a part does for a person, as the questions it answers. A catalogue component that describes its parts gets an Anatomy reference page.

mapping.title: Font size
mapping.question: typography.values
mapping.rule: size = base × ratio^step; display, title and heading snap to the 4px grid, other text rounds to whole px; set in rem, so text grows with the reader

jobs.title: Body size
jobs.how: Visual acuity → Body text sits where long reading stays effortless for this audience.

jobs.title: Other sizes
jobs.how: follows body size: size(n) = body × ratio^n, rounded to whole px
also: Weber's law → A ratio keeps each step equally easy to notice at any size.

jobs.title: Smallest text (dense data)
jobs.how: Visual acuity → 12px resolves at desk distance; dense data trades size for rows.

jobs.title: Contrast floor by size
jobs.how: Contrast sensitivity → From 24px, or 18.66px bold, text needs 3:1 instead of 4.5:1.

roles.to: set the size every other text steps from
roles.gets: long reading stays effortless

roles.to: rank titles and sections above the text by size
roles.gets: people see the order of a page before they read it

roles.to: give the one largest line on a page its own step
roles.gets: the key line or number is seen first

always_on.why: every scheme's type scale gives the display line a step of its own

roles.to: let names and secondary text step back from the body
roles.gets: labels and hints stay readable but quiet

roles.to: set numbers and values on a step of the scale
roles.gets: values read at a size the scale chose

always_on.why: every scheme's type scale gives values a step of their own

mapping.title: Line height
mapping.question: typography.definition
mapping.rule: line height = the ratio of the role's line kind (tight, snug or open) × its size; a kind with a grid snaps the line box to that grid

jobs.title: Open (body, data, captions)
jobs.how: Return sweep → Open leading lets the eye land on the right next line.

jobs.title: Tight (headings, labels)
jobs.how: Proximity → Heading lines closer than the space around them read as one unit.

jobs.title: Snug (short text that wraps)
jobs.how: Return sweep → Snug leading keeps a short block compact, with room enough to land on the next line.

jobs.title: Follow the size
jobs.how: follows typography.definition: line height = size × the role kind's ratio

jobs.title: Survive user spacing
jobs.how: follows text content: text box height = its content; no fixed heights

roles.to: hold the lines of a heading together
roles.gets: a heading that wraps still reads as one unit

roles.to: keep a label close to the thing it names
roles.gets: a label stays with its field, even when it wraps

roles.to: let the eye find the next line
roles.gets: people keep their place in text that wraps

mapping.title: Letter spacing
mapping.question: typography.definition
mapping.rule: letter spacing = extra space for uppercase labels only

jobs.title: Uppercase labels
jobs.how: Crowding → 5–12% extra space keeps capitals from crowding each other.

mapping.title: Font weight
mapping.question: typography.count
mapping.rule: weight shows rank, within the weights the typeface draws, and stays legible at its size

jobs.title: Rank the roles
jobs.how: Visual weight → Pair weight with size, so rank shows where sizes are close.

jobs.title: Weights the family draws
jobs.how: follows brand.q3 (typeface): weight steps = the family's drawn weights

jobs.title: Legible at small sizes
jobs.how: Visual acuity → Avoid thin weights at small sizes, where hairlines break up.

roles.to: show rank where sizes are close
roles.gets: headings stand out even one step above the text

roles.to: keep text legible at its size and below the headings in rank
roles.gets: small text keeps its strokes and its place in the order

jobs.title: Text step
jobs.how: Luminance contrast → Text steps are picked by contrast with their surface, never by hue.
also: follows accessibility.definition: first step with 4.5:1 (AA) or 7:1 (AAA) on its surface

jobs.title: Control edge and graphics
jobs.how: follows accessibility.definition: first step with 3:1 against its neighbours

jobs.title: Hover and pressed
jobs.how: follows the resting step: hover and pressed move along the same ramp

jobs.title: Minimum step gap
jobs.how: Perceptual uniformity → A minimum OKLCH lightness gap keeps two steps from looking alike.

jobs.title: Step curve convention
jobs.how: follows accessibility.definition: 400 steps apart = 3:1, 500 = 4.5:1, 700 = 7:1
also: Weber's law → Tight end steps give subtle tints; wide middle steps keep fills distinct.

jobs.title: Second contrast check
jobs.how: Contrast sensitivity → APCA weighs size, weight and polarity; the WCAG 2 ratio does not.

roles.role: a step of the neutral ramp
roles.to: give surfaces, lines and text one gray ramp to pick steps from
roles.gets: every gray in the product comes from one ramp, so no two grays clash

roles.role: text on the page's own surfaces
roles.to: keep words readable on every surface of the page
roles.gets: people read each line without strain

roles.role: the text on a filled color
roles.to: keep a label readable on the fill it sits on
roles.gets: a label on a button or a banner reads as clearly as body text

roles.role: a line or a control edge
roles.to: show where a control or a group ends
roles.gets: people find the edge of each field and each group

roles.to: show that the pointer is on an action
roles.gets: people see what they will press before they press it

jobs.title: Main action
jobs.how: Pre-attentive pop-out → High chroma on few elements finds them; overuse cancels it.

jobs.title: Chroma curve
jobs.how: follows color.values: chroma per step follows the muted, balanced or vivid curve

roles.to: make the action of a view easy to find
roles.gets: people find the next step at a glance

jobs.title: Hue set
jobs.how: follows brand hue: hues = brand hue + the scheme's harmony angles
also: Hue harmony → Set angles keep a chart inside the brand's color family.

jobs.title: Tell apart
jobs.how: Pre-attentive pop-out → A hue no other series uses lets the eye find a series at once.

jobs.title: Lightness steps (accessible first)
jobs.how: Redundant coding → A lightness step keeps pairs apart when hue fails.

jobs.title: Color difference
jobs.how: follows accent and status colors: ΔE ≥ threshold in 4 vision modes; measured, not set

jobs.title: Dashes and patterns
jobs.how: Redundant coding → A dash and a pattern separate series without any color.

roles.to: tell series and tags apart with no meaning attached
roles.gets: people match a series to its legend at once

always_on.why: a design system ships category colors for the products teams build

roles.to: group a tag or a block by color at low weight
roles.gets: tags stay quiet beside the content

always_on.why: a design system ships category colors for the products teams build

jobs.title: Convention hue
jobs.how: Learned convention → Red for danger and green for success register before the word.

jobs.title: Second cue
jobs.how: Redundant coding → An icon or a word carries status when hue fails.
also: follows accessibility.count: cues = color + word, or color + icon + word

jobs.title: Status steps
jobs.how: follows color-step: status steps meet the text and edge contrast rules

roles.to: show the state of something before the word is read
roles.gets: people see the risk at once, and an icon or a word carries it when hue fails

roles.role: the fill behind a status message
roles.to: mark the area of a message with its status
roles.gets: a banner reads as info, success, warning or danger at a glance

roles.role: status text on its own tint
roles.to: keep status text readable on its tint
roles.gets: the words of a message read as clearly as body text

jobs.title: Shared lines
jobs.how: Good continuation → One base step puts edges on shared lines, so layouts read ordered.

jobs.title: Density
jobs.how: Proximity → A smaller step fits more, until groups stop separating.

jobs.title: Units
jobs.how: follows the user's text size: text-bound values in rem; drawn detail in px

mapping.title: Gap, inset and padding
mapping.question: spacing.values
mapping.rule: gap or inset = the spacing base × the multiple of its use case (the base is 4px for small steps, 8px for big ones); a component spacing step = 4px × its multiplier × the rhythm, rounded to 4px, at most 64px

jobs.title: Gap inside a group
jobs.how: follows base step: gap.default = base × k; k grows from compact to spacious

jobs.title: Gap between groups
jobs.how: Proximity → The gap between groups is clearly larger than the gap inside one.

jobs.title: Control and cell inset
jobs.how: follows base step: inset = base × k, sized to the label's line height

jobs.title: Container padding
jobs.how: Common region → Content sits nearer its own edge than the next box.

jobs.title: Inside a component
jobs.how: follows spacing.values: map step = 4px × multiplier × the rhythm; x1 and x2 hold still, so rows stay tight

roles.to: keep the parts of one group together
roles.gets: people see which things belong together

roles.to: set one group or section apart from the next
roles.gets: people see where one group ends and the next begins

roles.role: the inset inside a control or a cell
roles.to: give a label room inside its box
roles.gets: a label never touches the edge of its control or cell

roles.to: keep content nearer its own edge than the next box
roles.gets: content reads as part of its own box

roles.role: a spacing step inside a component
roles.to: space the parts inside one component on one rhythm
roles.gets: every component spaces its parts the same way

mapping.title: Row height
mapping.question: spacing.roles
mapping.rule: row height = the default control height on the scheme's control scale

jobs.title: Default row
jobs.how: follows size.control.default: row = control default, unless the scheme sets its own

jobs.title: Compact row (scanning)
jobs.how: Working memory → Short rows put more records in view, so comparison needs no scroll.

jobs.title: Stay on the row
jobs.how: Good continuation → A clear row band leads the eye along one record.

jobs.title: Row as target
jobs.how: follows hit area: a clickable row meets the scheme's minimum target

roles.to: keep the eye on one record
roles.gets: people follow one record across a table

always_on.why: every scheme ships a table row, and a scheme without row heights takes the default control height

jobs.title: Mark controls
jobs.how: Similarity → One corner per kind makes controls a family the eye spots.

jobs.title: Tone
jobs.how: Curvature preference → Rounder controls read softer; the brand words are convention.

roles.to: mark every control as one family
roles.gets: people spot what they can press or type in

jobs.title: Object or cell
jobs.how: Uniform connectedness → Rounded surfaces read as separate objects; square ones tile.

roles.to: show whether a surface is an object or a cell
roles.gets: cards and panels read as separate objects, or tile as one grid

jobs.title: Option
jobs.how: follows radius.surface: option = surface − panel padding − border, floor 0

jobs.title: Element
jobs.how: follows radius.control: element = control; a moderate step if control is a pill

jobs.title: Badge
jobs.how: follows radius.control: badge = control, one step below, or pill

jobs.title: Nested formula
jobs.how: follows radius.surface: outer = inner + padding + border; at 24px+ padding, own corner

roles.role: the corner of an option in a menu
roles.to: keep an option's corner concentric with its menu
roles.gets: a highlighted option sits inside its menu as one shape

roles.role: the corner of a box inside a control
roles.to: keep a box that grows in the control's corner family
roles.gets: inputs and boxes that grow look like the controls beside them

roles.to: set a badge's corner from the control corner, or give it its own
roles.gets: badges belong to the same shape family as the controls

always_on.why: every scheme ships badges, and the roles answer decides whether the badge corner is its own or the control's

jobs.title: Default line
jobs.how: Common region → Where lines group, the line must show; where space groups, it stays thin.

jobs.title: Control edge
jobs.how: follows color-step (edge): a control's only edge takes the 3:1 edge step

jobs.title: Selected and invalid
jobs.how: Redundant coding → A thicker or colored edge adds a cue besides hue.

roles.role: the width of a default line
roles.to: show a line where lines group, and keep it thin where space groups
roles.gets: dividers and edges show where they must, without heavy boxes

always_on.why: every scheme draws dividers and control edges, and the layering answer decides how much work lines do

jobs.title: Depth order
jobs.how: Light from above → A larger offset and blur read as a higher layer.

jobs.title: Separate same-color surfaces
jobs.how: Figure and ground → A shade makes a same-color card the figure on its ground.

roles.to: lift a card off a ground of the same color
roles.gets: a card reads as one object on its page

always_on.why: every scheme ships a card layer, and the roles answer decides whether it casts a shadow

roles.role: the shadow of a floating layer
roles.to: set a menu, popover or dialog above the page
roles.gets: people see what floats and what it covers

always_on.why: every scheme ships a floating layer, and the roles answer decides whether it casts a shadow

jobs.title: Lightness ladder
jobs.how: follows surface.default: sunken < default < raised < floating, one step each
also: Lit surfaces → In dark mode, each higher surface is one step lighter.

jobs.title: Dark raised edge
jobs.how: Luminance contrast → A 1px light ring draws the edge a dark shadow cannot.

jobs.title: Dark-mode shadow
jobs.how: follows shadow: dark mode keeps shadows on floating layers only

roles.role: a rung of the surface ladder
roles.to: show what sits above what by lightness
roles.gets: people see the layers of a view without extra lines

roles.role: the reversed surface for short messages
roles.to: set a short message apart from the page
roles.gets: a toast or a tooltip stands out from the page

roles.role: the edge of a raised surface
roles.to: draw the edge of a raised surface where a shadow does not show
roles.gets: menus keep their shape in dark mode

jobs.title: Layer order
jobs.how: follows layer order: base < raised < sticky < overlay < modal < toast < tooltip

jobs.title: Scrim
jobs.how: Figure and ground → A dim layer behind a modal makes the dialog the figure.
also: follows surface ladder: scrim darkness comes from the scheme's surface ladder

roles.to: dim the page behind a dialog
roles.gets: the dialog is the one thing to act on

jobs.title: Productive
jobs.how: Response-time limits → Productive motion confirms the action and gets out of the way.

jobs.title: Expressive
jobs.how: Motion capture → Expressive motion draws the eye, so it is kept for brand moments.

roles.role: the time a panel takes to open
roles.to: let the eye follow a panel from its trigger to its place
roles.gets: people see where a menu or dialog comes from

always_on.why: every scheme opens panels, and with one speed a panel takes the feedback time

roles.role: the time a closing layer takes
roles.to: clear a closing layer out of the way fast
roles.gets: people get back to their work at once

roles.role: the time a launch moment takes
roles.to: give a brand moment room to be seen
roles.gets: a launch moment draws the eye once

jobs.title: Feedback
jobs.how: Response-time limits → At 150ms or less, feedback still feels caused by the click.

jobs.title: Panels
jobs.how: Object constancy → Up to 300ms lets the eye track a panel from origin to place.

jobs.title: Expressive moves
jobs.how: follows panel duration: expressive ≤ 500ms, the step above panels

roles.to: confirm an action while it still feels caused by the click
roles.gets: people see each action land and never wait for it

jobs.title: Enter
jobs.how: Physical motion → An arriving element decelerates to rest: ease-out.

jobs.title: Exit
jobs.how: follows feedback duration: productive: ease-out ~150ms; expressive: ease-in off-screen
also: Response-time limits → A strong ease-out does most of the move at once; it feels instant.

jobs.title: Transition
jobs.how: Object constancy → An ease-in-out keeps the element trackable from start to end.

jobs.title: Emphasize
jobs.how: Motion capture → Overshoot draws the eye, so only the emphasize move uses it.

roles.role: the easing of a change in place
roles.to: keep an element trackable while its state changes
roles.gets: people see a hover, a press or a toggle as one move

roles.role: the easing of a layer that appears
roles.to: bring an arriving layer to rest
roles.gets: a menu or dialog settles where people expect it

roles.role: the easing of a layer that leaves
roles.to: move a closing layer out of the way at once
roles.gets: a closing layer never holds people up

roles.role: the easing of a moment that calls for attention
roles.to: draw the eye to one moment, such as a success
roles.gets: people notice the moment that matters

always_on.why: every scheme names an emphasize move, and only the expressive family lets it overshoot

jobs.title: Reduced motion
jobs.how: Vestibular response → Remove travel and scale; fades and color changes stay.

jobs.title: Frequency gate
jobs.how: Habituation → No motion on keyboard actions or actions used 100+ times a day.

mapping.title: Icon size
mapping.question: iconography.values
mapping.rule: icon size = a size the icon set is drawn for (16, 20 or 24px), at least one label line tall; large icon size = larger than size.icon, where the scheme has two sizes

jobs.title: Match the label
jobs.how: follows label line height: icon = label line height, or the next size step

jobs.title: Recognize
jobs.how: Optical size → Use icons near the grid sizes they are drawn for: 16, 20 or 24px.

jobs.title: Meaningful icon
jobs.how: follows color-step (edge): a meaningful icon takes a 3:1 step

jobs.title: Lead a card
jobs.how: follows size.icon: large icon > size.icon, so it leads a card and never sits beside text

roles.role: the icon size next to text
roles.to: set an icon on the same line as its label
roles.gets: an icon and its word read as one item

roles.to: let an icon lead a card, a size above the icon beside text
roles.gets: the icon that leads a card stands apart from the icons beside words

mapping.title: Icon stroke
mapping.question: iconography.definition
mapping.rule: stroke width = the icon style's stroke on the icon set's 24px grid; it renders at stroke × icon size ÷ 24

jobs.title: One family
jobs.how: Similarity → One stroke, cap and join across the set make one family.

jobs.title: Rendered stroke
jobs.how: follows size.icon: rendered = stroke × icon size ÷ 24, never under 1px
also: Visual acuity → Thinner rendered lines break up and lose contrast.

jobs.title: Stroke by text weight
jobs.how: follows text weight: 1.5px regular; 2px medium or semibold; 2.5px bold

roles.to: draw every icon as one family
roles.gets: icons read as one set at every size

mapping.title: Control height
mapping.question: accessibility.values
mapping.rule: default height = the target the scheme's main input needs; compact and large = the default ± a step of the control scale; hit area = 24px for a pointer, else 44px

jobs.title: Default height
jobs.how: Fitts's law → The default sets the target for the scheme's main input device.

jobs.title: Compact
jobs.how: follows size.control.default: compact = one step below default on the control scale

jobs.title: Large
jobs.how: follows size.control.default: large = one step above default, or equal

jobs.title: Hit area
jobs.how: follows drawn size: hit = max(drawn, min target), no overlap; ≥ 24px, touch-first 44px

jobs.title: Align in a row
jobs.how: Good continuation → Controls of one height share edges, so a form row reads as one line.

jobs.title: Hold the text
jobs.how: follows label line height: min-height, not height: box = label line + inset

roles.to: give the main input device a target it hits
roles.gets: people hit a control on the first try

roles.to: fit controls into dense places, one step below the default
roles.gets: toolbars and tables hold controls that people can still hit

roles.to: give the main action one step more room, or the default
roles.gets: the main action is easy to find and to hit

roles.role: the hit area of a control
roles.to: keep a small control easy to hit
roles.gets: people hit small controls without a miss

jobs.title: Map states to channels
jobs.how: Redundant coding → Selected and invalid add weight, an edge or an icon to the hue.

jobs.title: Read-only
jobs.how: Luminance contrast → Read-only text keeps full contrast, because people still read it.
also: Common region → No field fill, so the value no longer reads as an input.

roles.to: show selection, hover and press on more than one channel
roles.gets: people see a state even when they cannot tell the hue

jobs.title: Disabled
jobs.how: Visual weight → Lower contrast reads as unavailable, with no opacity.
also: follows color-step: disabled = fixed muted steps, checked once per surface

jobs.title: Loading and dragging
jobs.how: Perceptual transparency → A see-through item reads as lifted above the page.
also: follows opacity: size stays; progress shows; opacity allowed

roles.role: a control that cannot be used
roles.to: show that a control is unavailable
roles.gets: people do not try an action that cannot work

jobs.title: Ring width
jobs.how: follows border-width.default: focus = one step heavier than the default line
also: Visual weight → The heaviest edge on the page draws the eye to focus.

jobs.title: Two-color gap
jobs.how: Luminance contrast → The gap takes the page color, so the ring keeps 3:1 on any fill.

jobs.title: Ring corner
jobs.how: follows radius.control: ring radius = control radius + offset

roles.to: show where the keyboard is
roles.gets: keyboard users never lose their place

roles.role: the width of the focus ring
roles.to: make focus the heaviest edge on the page
roles.gets: keyboard users see where they are

roles.role: the gap between a control and its focus ring
roles.to: keep the page color between the ring and the control
roles.gets: the ring keeps its contrast on any fill

mapping.title: Typeface
mapping.question: brand.q3
mapping.rule: font family = the face the typeface answer names for the role

jobs.title: Carry the product
jobs.how: Voice and legibility → The scheme's answer names the faces and why they fit its readers.

roles.to: carry the product's voice in every text role
roles.gets: the product reads as itself on every screen
